messages.subject_clean: error in estimating genotype error rate
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am following on page 35 of "Genetic map construction with R/qtl" the
commands to estimate the genotyping error rate from my data.

I followed the commands on page 35 to the letter (using my own cross
object of course):

loglik <- err <- c(0.001, 0.0025, 0.005, 0.0075, 0.01, 0.0125, 0.015,
0.0175, 0.02)
for(i in seq(along=err)) {
	cat(i, "of", length(err), "\n")
	tempmap <- est.map(aa_clean_lg25, error.prob=err[i])
	loglik[i] <- sum(sapply(tempmap, attr, "loglik"))
}

However, I get this error message:

Error in sum(sapply(tempmap, attr, "loglik")) :
  invalid 'type' (list) of argument
Execution halted

The cross object I am currently trying to estimate the genotyping
error of has had its linkage groups formed and rf estimated, but its
markers haven't been ordered yet. However, I've also tried using a
cross object which has had its markers ordered on all chromosomes and
I got the same error message.

In trying to debug, but as an R newbie I'm hitting a wall. Am I
getting this error message because sum() doesn't take in list
arguments? (it only takes in numeric or complex or logical vectors,
according to the documentation) If so, should I use as.vector() to
convert the value of sapply() from a list into a numeric, complex, or
logical vector?

Thanks so much for any advice!

messages.body_plain:
The code assumes that you're working with multiple linkage groups, and so

    sum(sapply(tempmap, attr, "loglik"))

is pulling out and then summing the log likelihoods for each linkage group, to give an overall log likelihood.

But even with one linkage group, you'd have to do something like this, though

    loglik[i] <- attr(tempmap[[1]], "loglik")

should work.

But I don't really understand the error, as sapply should return a vector rather than a list.

Perhaps you could privately email me the file from

    save(aa_clean_lg25, file="lg25.RData")

so I could reproduce and study the problem.

Or you might try adding a print statement in there to see what it's trying to sum:

   print(sapply(tempmap, attr, "loglik"))

karl

Best Regards,
Josh

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have a very large F2 cross dataset I am using to build a linkage
map. Following "Genetic map construction with R/QTL", I've gone
through all the recommended cleaning steps and have a final cross
object of ~9000 markers and 51 individuals. formLinkageGroups() put
the markers into about 20 different linkage groups (and a number of
singletons), which is what we expect from this species.

However, I've found that ordering the markers on each linkage group is
very time-consuming. I am fortunate to have access to a large computer
cluster to run these commands, but ordering the markers on a linkage
group which had ~300 markers took 2.5 hours.

Considering I have 17 more linkage groups which I need to order the
markers of, including 1 linkage group with ~1000 markers on it, I'm
wondering if it's possible to split up my current cross object into 17
different cross objects, each containing 1 linkage group. Then, I
could submit parallel jobs to our cluster to order markers on
different linkage groups at the same time, and once each linkage group
is done ordering, I would hope to be able to put the linkage groups
back together again into one cross object.

>From what I've read so far about the internal data structure of R/QTL
in Karl's book, I want to venture a guess that this may be feasible,
although I could be entirely wrong. I mainly don't know what commands
I would use to put the linkage groups back together again...I may have
to try and code something in R myself for that I'm guessing.

Any thoughts or insights on this would be appreciated (especially from
Karl :)

Thanks!

Best,

Elisa

messages.body_plain:
You can work with each chromosome separately and then use switch.order() to re-order the markers in the original cross object to match those you've discovered.

Here's a bit of code, as an example.  First, I load the hyper data and re-order markers on chromosome 4.  We'll pretend that hyper.new <http://hyper.new> has the marker order we want

  data(hyper)
  hyper.new <http://hyper.new> <- switch.order(hyper, chr=4, c(3,1,2,5,4,6:nmar(hyper)[4]))

Now I want to get the markers in hyper to match the new order in hyper.new <http://hyper.new>.  I use match and then switch.order

  m <- match(markernames(hyper.new <http://hyper.new>, chr=4), markernames(hyper, chr=4))
  hyper.reordered <- switch.order(hyper, 4, m)

I would also suggest using findDupMarkers() to identify markers with matching genotypes, and then drop.markers to omit them before you do the map construction.  Markers with the same data will end up in the same spot anyway, and their presence will just slow everything down.

  dupmar <- findDupMarkers(hyper)
  hyper.nodup <- drop.markers(hyper, unlist(dupmar))

karl

messages.body_plain:

> I have a colleague who is a statistical geneticist and a computational biologist by training and he didn't think any additional QTL found by stepwise selection would be very significant, suggesting that perhaps these QTL are only significant when they are additive, i.e. the model as a whole is significant, but individually, the QTL may not be, in which case reporting them as QTL is misleading. I am wondering if it is worth reporting these stepwise models over/in addition to the QTL identified using scanone?

The logic seems circular here.  If one thinks that only QTL that are individually significant are worth reporting, then those found from multiple QTL modeling using stepwiseqtl() are not worth it.

The reasons for considering QTL from multiple QTL modeling (detailed in the literature) include:
(1) reducing background variation from strong or moderate QTL
(2) detecting QTLs that interact (epistasis)
(3) accurately localizing linked QTL (to avoid ghost QTL)

That said, multiple QTL modeling is more involved, and there are some risks there.  So, one should examine the QTLs found carefully and convince oneself that they are not the result of any artifacts in the data.  One problem I have encountered a few times is outliers in the phenotype.  These may lead one to conclude that there are more QTL than the data really support.

>
> I also see more QTL added by stepwiseqtl() when I use a denser marker coverage (7 markers/cM) but they drop out when I use a subset of that genotype data (1 marker/cM), which further reduces my confidence in the biological reality of QTL identified using this function. Do you have any thoughts on this?
>

 Denser markers are more informative, so from that point of view one should find more QTL with the denser set.  That said, the informativeness of 7 markers per cM should not be very different from 1 marker per cM unless you have RI lines (in which case it would be somewhat different).  You may want to redo the stepwise with a lower threshold (maybe some QTL missed the threshold by a whisker).  You should also check for outliers in the phenotype.

Cheers,
Saunak

The multiple imputations are not intended to be output to a file, but only used in functions like scanone and effectplot.

The main difficulty in writing them to a file will be that they constitute a 3-dimensional table: individual x position x imputation.  They are split apart by chromosome in the cross object; see page 44 in the R/qtl book (http://www.rqtl.org/book).

You can use the function pull.draws to pull them out as a 3-dimensional array, but it's not obvious how to write these to a file.

> data(hyper)
> hyper <- sim.geno(hyper, step=2, n.draws=64)
> dr <- pull.draws(hyper)
> dim(dr)
[1] 250 810  64

Regarding the second question, "is n.draws=64 large enough?"  It depends on (a) what you're trying to do and (b) how dense and complete your genotype data are.  In general, I'd say, do the imputations again and look at how much the final results change.  If they don't change substantially, then you're probably doing sufficient imputations.

Say you see two peaks in the scanone result and you pick off the biggest one as a QTL and then run addqtl on that chromosome.  If the second peak goes away after conditioning on the first peak, what would you say?  I'd probably be satisfied with the one QTL.

Consider also item 21 in the FAQ (http://www.rqtl.org/faq):

Q: How can I pick out multiple peaks on a chromosome from the output of scanone?

A: It is best not to rely on the results of scanone to infer the presence of multiple linked QTL. Instead, one should consider the results of a two-dimensional, two-QTL scan (with scantwo) or multiple QTL analysis (with fitqtl and/or scanqtl).

Nevertheless, if there are a couple of peaks on a chromosome, and one wishes to identify the location of the second peak, one can subset the results fromscanone to find the location of the second peak. For example, if out contains the output from scanone, and one wishes to find the location for the peak on chromosome 1 that is distal to 50 cM on the genetic map, one may use code like the following.

> max(out[out$chr==1 & out$pos > 50,])

messages.body_plain:
You can align things with a bit of R code, using movemarker()

Say x1 and x2 are the two crosses, and you want the markers in x2 to be in the same organized as they are in x1.

    x2.fixed <- x2

    # locations of x2 markers in cross x1
    pos <- find.markerpos(x1, markernames(x2))

    # for those found, move to position in x1
    for(i in which(!is.na <http://is.na>(pos[,1])) )
      x2.fixed <- movemarker(x2.fixed, rownames(pos)[i], pos[i,1], pos[i,2])

    # perhaps drop the markers that weren't in x1
    x2.fixed <- drop.markers(x2.fixed, rownames(pos)[is.na <http://is.na>(pos[,1])])

    # probably need to sort the chromosomes
    x2.fixed$geno <- x2.fixed$geno[names(x1$geno)]

The last line won't work if x1 has linkage groups whose markers are not in x2.  Let me know if you need further explanation or clarification.

messages.body_plain:
fatScan

I think it might be a bug because it sounds a lot like this (from www.rqtl.org/BUGS.txt <http://www.rqtl.org/BUGS.txt>):

"2. Bug in checkcovar (in util.R) regarding omitting individuals with
      missing phenotypes when there's an ID column with numeric values.
      The wrong individuals get omitted from the cross. [Fixed in
      Version 1.24-9.]"

> nphe(f2g)
[1] 16
> sum(!is.na <http://is.na>(f2g$pheno[,8]))
[1] 842
> sum(!is.na <http://is.na>(sex))
[1] 2054

> sum(!is.na <http://is.na>(f2g$pheno[,8]) & !is.na <http://is.na>(sex))

[1] 842

I am working on a cluster so I have limited control over software versions (but I'll see if I can update it).

Thanks for the response
Justin
